Newborn Care

Goat’s rue for breast milk: evidence and safety

Updated: November 8, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Goat’s rue is sold as a way to increase breast milk, but a long history of use is not the same as reliable evidence. Studies have not established that the herb alone improves milk production, and information about its safety for breastfeeding parents and babies is very limited. Before trying it, have concerns about feeding assessed and discuss the exact product with a clinician or pharmacist. A tea, capsule or ‘natural’ label does not remove the uncertainty.

Identify the plant behind the name

The herb discussed here is Galega officinalis, commonly called goat’s rue. It belongs to the legume family, Fabaceae, which also includes fenugreek. Common names can vary, so check the botanical name on a product rather than assuming that similarly named herbs are interchangeable. Being in the same plant family does not show that two herbs have the same effect on milk supply.

Galega officinalis is native to parts of Europe, North Africa and western Asia. It was introduced into the United States as a forage plant in the 1890s, but its alkaloids can poison livestock. Accounts of traditional use to stimulate milk production, lower glucose or treat illnesses such as tuberculosis are historical uses, not evidence that it is an effective or appropriate treatment for those conditions.

What the milk-supply research can tell us

LactMed’s October 2026 review found no scientifically valid clinical trials supporting goat’s rue alone as a galactogogue, meaning a substance intended to increase milk production. An old study in five breastfeeding mothers found no improvement, while other early reports lacked adequate controls. Those designs cannot reliably show whether an apparent change came from the herb, normal changes after birth or feeding support.

Some newer research tested combinations. A randomized study in 100 mothers of preterm infants reported higher milk production with a product containing silymarin, phosphatidylserine and galega than with placebo. It cannot establish that galega was responsible or that a different tea or capsule will do the same. A product survey also reported that many users felt their supply increased, but perceived improvement is not an objective measurement or proof of effectiveness.

Breast growth and induced lactation remain unproven claims

There is no established clinical evidence that goat’s rue regrows breast tissue, repairs damage from breast surgery or reliably enables someone to breastfeed an adopted baby. Personal reports and marketing claims do not answer those questions. A lack of good research also means that a response cannot be predicted for an individual; it is not a reason to promise that trying a higher amount will work.

If you have had breast surgery, suspect limited milk-producing tissue or want to induce lactation, ask for an individualized plan with a clinician and a skilled lactation professional. The plan needs to consider your history, breast stimulation or milk removal, and the baby’s nutritional needs. The Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine does not recommend a particular galactogogue for everyone, and a supplement should not delay that assessment.

Fresh, dried and encapsulated do not mean the same as safe

Do not harvest or prepare fresh goat’s rue for self-treatment. Its toxicity in animals is well documented, and drying is not a reliable safety switch: a published report described suspected poisoning in two horses after exposure through hay containing Galega officinalis. Animal poisoning cannot tell us a safe or lethal dose for a breastfeeding person, but it contradicts a simple claim that only the fresh plant can be hazardous.

Dried leaves, teas and capsules have not been shown to be safe for every breastfeeding parent or infant. LactMed found no published measurements of goat’s rue components in human milk or breastfed infants at its latest revision. That is missing information, not evidence that the baby receives none. A manufacturer’s recommended amount or a quality seal cannot establish breastfeeding safety or clinical benefit.

Understand the possible effect on blood glucose

Goat’s rue contains guanidine-related compounds, including galegine, that may lower blood glucose. The size of this effect with a particular supplement is uncertain. This matters especially if you have diabetes, a history of low blood sugar, or use insulin or another medicine that lowers glucose. Adding the herb could complicate treatment; it should not be used as a substitute for prescribed diabetes care.

Discuss the product with your prescriber or pharmacist before taking it, and do not alter prescribed medicines to make room for it. Shaking, sweating, a racing heart, weakness or confusion can be symptoms of low blood sugar. Follow your established treatment plan if you have one and seek medical advice about new episodes. Severe confusion, a seizure, unconsciousness or inability to swallow safely needs emergency help; do not give food or drink to an unconscious person.

Allergies and mixed-product reports need careful interpretation

A herbal ingredient can cause an allergic reaction, and a blend may contain several potential allergens. Tell your clinician about previous reactions to herbs, foods and medicines and show the full ingredient list. Although goat’s rue shares a plant family with peanuts, soy and fenugreek, that fact alone does not prove that everyone allergic to one of them will react to goat’s rue. Do not test an unfamiliar supplement yourself after a serious allergy history.

LactMed describes adverse events involving products or teas with several herbs, including reports of maternal digestive or liver problems and two young infants with lethargy, poor feeding and vomiting. These reports do not establish that goat’s rue caused the events; other ingredients and unmeasured exposure limit interpretation. They also do not justify declaring a mixture harmless because an individual ingredient has not been proved responsible.

Laboratory findings are not treatments for other illnesses

Goat’s rue extracts have been investigated in laboratory research, including antibacterial testing. One medicinal-plant study also used a potato-disc tumor assay, which is not a trial of cancer treatment in people. Activity in bacteria or a laboratory model does not show that swallowing the herb treats an infection or cancer, or that exposure is safe during breastfeeding.

Claims about using the plant as a diuretic, treating tuberculosis or managing diabetes likewise should not replace medical diagnosis or prescribed treatment. A glucose-lowering effect can be a hazard rather than a useful treatment when the product’s dose and effects are uncertain. The evidence reviewed does not establish these advertised or traditional uses as safe, effective reasons to take goat’s rue while breastfeeding.

There is no established safe tea recipe or capsule dose

Research does not provide a validated goat’s rue dose or preparation that can be recommended as safe and effective during breastfeeding. A teaspoon of dried leaves is not a standardized dose, and the contents of capsules can vary. Recipes that specify cups per day or suggest combining goat’s rue with fennel, nettle, alfalfa or blessed thistle add uncertainty rather than solving it.

Bring the packaging, ingredient list and amount already taken to a clinician or pharmacist. Include any other teas, medicines and supplements. Avoid starting or combining herbal products on your own during pregnancy or breastfeeding. If you are already using one, seek advice about stopping it and assessing any symptoms; do not stop a prescribed medicine or assume you must end breastfeeding solely because you used a supplement.

Keep the feeding assessment more important than the herb

If you are worried about supply, ask someone qualified to assess milk transfer, the feeding or expressing pattern, and your baby’s growth and hydration. Effective, regular milk removal and treatment of an underlying problem matter more than adding an unproven herb. This is particularly important when a baby is premature, unwell or struggling to gain weight, because waiting for a supplement to work can delay needed feeding support.

If supply is already adequate or excessive, there is no reason to try to increase it with goat’s rue. The herb has not been proved to cause oversupply or mastitis, so those complications should not be presented as a predictable effect. However, uncomfortable fullness, a painful breast or an unsettled feeding pattern deserves appropriate assessment rather than automatically adding another milk-promoting product.

Know when symptoms need prompt or emergency help

Stop taking a suspected herbal product and seek prompt medical advice if you or your baby develop new symptoms after exposure. New poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, repeated vomiting or worsening illness in a young baby needs assessment without waiting to see whether the supplement helps. Keep the product packaging and tell the clinician what was taken, when, and what else was used; the timing alone does not prove the cause.

Call local emergency services for trouble breathing, swelling of the tongue or throat, collapse or another severe allergic reaction. Use a prescribed adrenaline auto-injector if available and follow its instructions. A baby who is floppy, difficult to wake, struggling to breathe or turning blue or grey also needs emergency help. Severe low-blood-sugar symptoms require urgent treatment even if it is unclear whether goat’s rue contributed.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Separate research on Galega officinalis alone from mixed products, surveys and traditional claims.

Do not infer human breastfeeding safety from drying, packaging, laboratory activity or lack of measured milk levels.

Assess feeding concerns and review the exact product, medicines, glucose risks and any new symptoms.

How BeMama can help

A useful next step is a feeding assessment and a product review, not a stronger tea or a larger dose of an uncertain herb.

When to seek help

Do not self-treat with fresh goat’s rue or assume dried products are safe. Severe allergy, collapse, seizures, inability to swallow safely or a baby who is floppy, difficult to wake or struggling to breathe requires emergency help. Do not replace prescribed diabetes treatment with the herb.

Evidence notes updated: November 8, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Goat’s rue is Galega officinalis; similar names or shared plant families do not prove equivalent effects.
  • Reliable evidence for the herb alone increasing breast milk is lacking; combination trials cannot isolate its contribution.
  • Dried herbs, teas and capsules are not established as safe during breastfeeding, and milk exposure has not been measured.
  • Possible glucose lowering, allergies and other symptoms deserve attention; do not replace prescribed treatment with the herb.
  • There is no validated safe dose or recipe. Get feeding concerns assessed and review the exact product with a clinician.

Frequently asked questions

What is goat’s rue?

Goat’s rue is Galega officinalis, a legume-family plant sold in some teas and supplements intended to increase milk supply. It has a history of traditional use, but the botanical identity, product ingredients and evidence matter more than the common name or marketing description.

What benefits of goat’s rue have been proved?

Good clinical evidence has not established that goat’s rue alone increases milk production, grows breast tissue or makes induced lactation successful. Studies of mixtures and surveys do not settle those questions. Laboratory antibacterial or tumor-assay findings also do not establish it as a treatment for infection or cancer in people.

How should goat’s rue be taken during breastfeeding?

There is no established safe and effective breastfeeding dose or tea recipe. Do not assume that dried leaves or capsules are safe or combine several herbs to increase the effect. Discuss the exact product with a clinician or pharmacist and arrange an assessment of milk-supply concerns before self-treatment.

Who should be particularly cautious about goat’s rue?

Anyone considering it during pregnancy or breastfeeding needs advice because safety is uncertain. A history of low blood sugar, diabetes treatment, serious allergies, other medicines or a premature or unwell baby makes individual assessment especially important. This does not imply that use is proven safe for everyone else.

Is dried goat’s rue safer than the fresh plant?

Drying does not establish safety. Animal poisoning has been reported after exposure through hay, and there is no validated safe breastfeeding dose for dried leaves or capsules. Animal reports cannot be used to calculate a safe human dose or prove that every human exposure will cause harm.

Can goat’s rue rebuild breast tissue after surgery?

That benefit has not been established in clinical research. Breast surgery and difficulties establishing milk production need an individual lactation and medical assessment. Do not rely on a supplement to repair tissue or postpone a plan that meets the baby’s nutritional needs.

What if I already took goat’s rue?

Keep the packaging and contact a clinician or pharmacist with the ingredients, amount and timing, especially if you or the baby have symptoms. An exposure is not proof that harm has occurred, and it does not automatically mean breastfeeding must end. Severe allergy symptoms, collapse, seizures, or a baby who is floppy, difficult to wake or struggling to breathe need emergency care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
